newsitem.title: USA: Jobless rate up, payrolls off, economy cool.
newsitem.headline: Jobless rate up, payrolls off, economy cool.

text.p: The nation's unemployment rate edged up to 5.2 percent last month from 5.1 percent as jobs vanished for the first time in eight months, the government said Friday, reflecting an end-of-summer economic cool-down.

In the government's first assessment of the economy's health in September, the Labour Department said the number of non-farm jobs unexpectedly shrank by 40,000 during the month, after payrolls grew by 241,000 in August. Economists, on average, had expected an increase of 166,000 jobs last month.

The report, which cheered inflation-worried stock and bond markets by depicting a weaker job market, was seen by economists as exaggerating the economy's late-summer slowdown, which has been most pronounced in manufacturing.

"This report grossly overstates what's occurred," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant for Northern Trust Co. in Chicago. "But there is evidence that the rapid growth of spring has given way to a more measured growth pace."
The Clinton adminstration saw the report, the next-to-last measure of the job market before the Nov. 5 elections, as evidence of a steadily growing, low-inflation economy.

"All recent indicators suggest that the economy will continue on a healthy and balanced course of low unemployment, low inflation and solid economic growth, with all Americans increasingly sharing in the benefits," said White House Council of Economic Advisers Chairman Joseph Stiglitz.

The evidence of September's weaker job market came a week after Federal Reserve policy makers decided to leave interest rates unchanged to the surprise of analysts who had expected a pre-emptive rate rise to relieve upward price pressures.
Economist David Wyss of DRI/McGraw-Hill in Lexington, Mass., said lurking inflationary pressures eventually will force the Fed to tighten credit.
"I think the Fed has to tighten, but this report takes the urgency out of it," said Wyss.

Workers' average hourly earnings, which have been closely watched for signs that wage increases may start to push consumer prices higher, rose by 6 cents last month to $11.92 after rising 5 cents in August. Over the past year, they rose 3.5 percent.
"Earnings are moving higher, but they're not moving higher at an alarming rate," said economist Richard Berner of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.

"The good news for American workers is that pay increases are running ahead of inflation," Berner said. "But the bad news for companies is that they're having difficulty passing along those pay increases in their prices."
Over the past year, job growth has averaged nearly 200,000 a month. But in the July-September third quarter the average growth rate retreated to 145,000 a month.
Last month's job drop, the first since a decline of 66,000 jobs in January, was led by declines of 57,000 factory jobs and 67,000 local public school jobs, the department said.

In the slowing industrial sector, manufacturing employment has declined by 331,000 since March 1995. Last month, the factory work week rose by 6 minutes to 41.8 hours, while overtime was unchanged at 4.5 hours a week.

With last month's drop in public school jobs, employment in service businesses such as stores, restaurants, government, and financial services grew by a mere 10,000 after expanding by 211,000 in August.

The department attributed the teaching job drop to a statistical distortion in its method of seasonally adjusting data caused by earlier starts in the school year. The number of local teaching jobs rose by 85,000 in August.

"This accounts for the large increases, on a seasonally adjusted basis, in local education employment over the summer and for this month's sharp decline," said Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics.
Job growth slowed in construction, temporary help and retail trade, but rose in health care, the department said.

The department's survey of households showed that more people entered the job market last month as the civilian labour force, which includes employed workers and those seeking jobs, grew by 455,000 to 134.34 million.
The number of jobless workers rose by 141,000 last month to 6.97 million, while those with jobs rose by 313,000 to 127.37 million, it said.
